topic: Microsaccades: constant tiny eye movements stop vision from fading

slides.title: Tiny constant jumps
slides.body: Even when you stare, your eyes make tiny jumps called microsaccades.

slides.title: Freeze them, lose sight
slides.body: In lab tests, images held perfectly still on the retina fade away.

slides.title: Built for change
slides.body: Your eye's nerve cells respond to change. No change, and they go quiet.

caption:
Right now, while you read this, your eyes are jumping about once or twice a second. These tiny jumps are called microsaccades, and you never notice them.

They're not a glitch. In lab experiments where an image was locked perfectly still on the retina, people saw it fade away within seconds. Your vision depends on constant motion.

Part 2 tomorrow: an illusion that lets you see this fading for yourself. Follow so you don't miss it. Source: Martinez-Conde et al., Nature Reviews Neuroscience (2004).

Did you know your eyes were moving all the time?
